en: Netti:
The Section on Exposition of the Counter-Demonstrations (Paṭiniddesavāra Vibhaṅga) 8
The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Analysis (Vibhattihāravibhaṅga).
Therein, what is the mode of conveying analysis?
It is: “The Dhamma, the proximate cause, and the plane.”
There are two types of discourses: those conducive to spiritual cultivation (*vāsanābhāgiya*) and those conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
There are two types of practice: that which partakes of merit (*puññabhāgiyā*) and that which partakes of the fruit (*phalabhāgiyā*).

There are two types of virtue: the virtue of restraint (*saṃvarasīla*) and the virtue of abandonment (*pahānasīla*). In this regard, the Blessed One [taught] the discourse conducive to spiritual cultivation for the sake of the practice partaking of merit...
He teaches the practice; established in the virtue of restraint, he becomes a practitioner of the holy life through that holy life.
In this regard, the Blessed One teaches a discourse pertaining to penetration by means of the practice pertaining to the fruit;
established in the virtue of abandoning, he becomes a practitioner of the holy life through that holy life.
In this context, what is the discourse dealing with purification (vāsanābhāgiya-sutta)?

A discourse dealing with purification is one that consists of talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven, the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation.
In this context, what is the discourse dealing with penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta)?

A discourse pertaining to penetration (*Nibbedhabhāgiya*) is one that proclaims the Four Noble Truths. In a discourse pertaining to the habitual tendency (*Vāsanābhāgiya*), there is no full understanding, no path, and no fruit.
In a discourse pertaining to penetration, there is full understanding, there is the path, and there is the fruit.
These are the four types of discourses.

By means of the fruit, virtue, and holy life resulting from the teaching of these four discourses, and by investigating through the method of "all-inclusive search," one should apply them according to the method of "logical connection" for as far as the range of knowledge extends.
In this regard, which phenomena are common?
Two phenomena are common: commonality of name and commonality of physical basis.
Or whatever else of this kind there may be: the defilements to be abandoned by vision are common to both beings fixed in falsehood and beings not so fixed;
sensual lust and ill-will are common to both the worldling and the stream-enterer;
and the higher fetters are common to both the worldling and the non-returner—whatever such things there may be.
When a noble disciple enters a mundane attainment, it is shared with those who are not free from lust;
for shared phenomena do not thus exceed one another's respective domains.
Even one who is endowed with these qualities does not transcend that state.
These phenomena are common.
In this regard, which phenomena are uncommon?

They are to be sought in relation to the teaching, concerning those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*), the capable and the incapable, and the person of the eighth stage (*aṭṭhamaka*) and the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).

Sensual desire and ill will are common natural laws for some, but not for others; the higher fetters of a person on the eighth stage and of a non-returner are common natural laws for some, but not for others.
The name "all those in training" is a common natural law for all, but not for others.
The name "practitioner" is common to all, while the natural law (dhammatā) is not common.
The training-ethic (sekkhasīla) of all those in training (sekkha) is common, while the natural law is not common.
Thus, one who perceives distinctions should investigate by way of the inferior, superior, and middling.
The plane of seeing is the proximate cause for entering the path of certainty; the plane of development is the proximate cause for attaining the higher fruits;
the painful practice with slow direct knowledge is the proximate cause for serenity; the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge is the proximate cause for insight;
and the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving is the proximate cause for the voice of another.

The basis for the common ground is the basis for the wisdom consisting of reflection; the basis for the basis of meritorious action consisting in virtue is the basis for the wisdom consisting of reflection;
the basis for the basis of meritorious action consisting in mental development is the basis for the wisdom consisting of mental development.
The basis for the basis of meritorious action consisting in generosity is the basis for both the voice of another and the wisdom consisting of what has been heard.
The basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting in virtue is the common proximate cause for wisdom consisting in reflection and for appropriate attention;
the basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting in cultivation is the common proximate cause for wisdom consisting in cultivation and for right view.
Living in a suitable locality is the common proximate cause for both seclusion and concentration;
reliance on noble persons is the common proximate cause for the three kinds of verified confidence and for serenity;
right direction of oneself is the common proximate cause for moral shame and insight; and the relinquishing of the unwholesome is the proximate cause for the investigation of the wholesome.
The well-expounded nature of the Dhamma is the common proximate cause for both the faculty of concentration and the planting of roots of merit;
the well-practiced nature of the Saṅgha is the common proximate cause for both the excellence of the Saṅgha and the attainment of the fruits [of the path];
and the perfection of the Teacher is the common proximate cause for the inspiring of faith in those without it and for the further increase of faith in those who already possess it.

The common proximate cause is the unassailable nature of the Pātimokkha; it is the common proximate cause for the restraint of persons who are difficult to manage and for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved persons.
Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "The Dhamma and its proximate cause."
The Mode of Conveying Analysis is concluded.
